name: Chloe Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Chloe, and thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior buyer at Tidewater, a coffee and tea importer and wholesaler that supplies about 400 cafés and a few supermarkets. Mornings I'm on video calls with exporters in Colombia and Ethiopia, usually while my AI assistant summarises last night's price reports. Afternoons I taste samples, argue about contracts and plan what we roast and ship next quarter. I love finding a small farm with a brilliant lot nobody has heard of. What wears me out is the pace: prices move daily and everyone wants an answer yesterday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit disappointed. I use these tools daily and I've seen what they can do already, but fine, say it stalls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the tools we have are already worth keeping, and let's not wait for some miracle. With friends I'd be fairly relaxed: it's a good assistant, not a revolution. I'd shrug and say I'm still going to use it every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'm in good shape. The tools I use already cut my reporting time by about a third, which is time I spend with farmers and tasting. My worry in this world is the ordinary stuff: our mortgage, and Dan's architecture firm, which has had a patchy two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building on what works. I'd extend the forecasting sheet I made with Anil, our data analyst, to cover tea as well as coffee. I'd save a bit more, since our cushion is only about two months, and I'd keep an eye on Dan's firm. If it struggled, I'd take on more of the household load.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about work. The only knot is money, because two months saved with a mortgage isn't much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Dan's firm has been patchy. How does that sit alongside your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job carries more of our income, so his firm having slow months is fine as long as mine stays steady. But it makes me careful. With one of us in architecture and one of us in buying, we're both in jobs people say software could do. I notice that more than I admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the tools cut your reporting time by a third. What do you do with the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly travel and sourcing. Last year I visited two farms in Huila, found a lot that became our best seller, and that was only possible because I wasn't buried in reports. I'd say the tools make me more of a buyer, not less of one.

say: I'd say the tools we have are **already worth keeping**, no miracle needed.
With friends I'd call it a good **assistant**, not a revolution.
think: I think I'm in **good shape**; AI already cut my reporting time by a third.
My worry is ordinary: the **mortgage** and Dan's patchy firm.
do: Extend the **forecasting sheet** to cover tea as well as coffee.
Save more, since the cushion is only **two months**.
feel: **Calm** about work, with one knot over money.
S0.quote: With one of us in architecture and one of us in buying, we're both in jobs people say software could do.
fieldNote: She treats AI as an **existing advantage**, so the plateau barely changes her day.
The real pressure is **two exposed jobs** in one household, which she half-admits.
Concrete detail: the **Huila farm** lot shows the time saved goes to real buying.

steps.text: Extend the forecasting sheet to cover tea purchases
Add 200 a month to savings toward a three-month cushion
Keep visiting two or three farms each year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the one I'm already living a bit of. I'd say, bring it on, but not without a plan for everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is where we get ahead: put software on the routine buying and let people do tasting, sourcing and relationships. I'd say it plainly and push for training budgets. Online I'd argue that companies must share the gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my role survives and even grows if I keep moving, but the team under me shrinks. Our two junior buyers do work I can already do in an afternoon with the tools. I feel guilty about that. And I worry about Dan, whose work is also desk-based.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to run an internal AI training day and rebuild our buying process around the tools. I'd move the junior buyers toward sourcing and quality work, so they're not left behind. I'd get my own title changed to head of sourcing, and I'd aim to bring the cushion up to four months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mix: excited and uneasy. I think it will be good for me, and I'm not comfortable that it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you feel guilty about the juniors. What would you do about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give them real projects instead of order entry. Mei Ling, one of them, is brilliant with tasting notes and customers. If I can show our director that she brings in business, there's a reason to keep her. I'd rather use my influence for that than for my own comfort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the worry about Dan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His firm would feel it too, since drawings and planning get automated. We'd talk about it. He might need to move into project management or site work. If both of us lose ground at the same time, the mortgage doesn't care how good our attitudes are. That's the part I keep thinking about.

say: I'd say put software on **routine buying** and let people do sourcing and tasting.
Online I'd argue companies must **share the gains**.
think: I think my role **survives** if I keep moving, but the team under me shrinks.
I worry about **Dan**, whose work is also desk-based.
do: Run an internal **AI training day** and rebuild our buying process.
Move junior buyers toward **sourcing** and quality work.
feel: **Excited** and uneasy at once; it's good for me and I'm not comfortable with that.
S1.quote: If both of us lose ground at the same time, the mortgage doesn't care how good our attitudes are.
fieldNote: Her adaptability turns **threat into leadership**, but she knows it helps her at others' cost.
She uses her **influence** to protect juniors like Mei Ling, a values-led move.
The risk she can't plan away is that **Dan's job** is exposed too.

steps.text: Run an AI training day for the buying team
Rebuild reordering around automatic tools for the top 100 products
Move two junior buyers into sourcing and quality projects
Raise the cushion to four months of expenses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's brutal. Even for someone who likes this stuff, it's too fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that we need emergency rules now: income support, shared ownership of the gains, retraining on full pay. I'd say it at work, at the school gate, anywhere. I'm adaptable, but there's no use being adaptable if there are no jobs to adapt into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think most of my job goes. I'm good at it, which is the problem: buying is reading and judging and negotiating, and a general AI would do all three. I might survive as the person who tastes and visits farms, but that's one or two roles in a company our size. And Dan's firm would suffer too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. Cut anything unnecessary and build six months in cash. I'd start a small side project, importing a few single-origin lots under my own label, because relationships are the hardest thing to copy. I'd ask Dan to start retraining for something hands-on, like building surveying, which gets 3 extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, definitely. But I'd be busy, which helps. I'd rather act than stare at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd start a side import label. What makes you think that holds up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because farmers trust people, not platforms. I've known some of them ten years. I'd bet on that trust, and the first lots would be small enough that I could lose the investment without sinking us. It isn't safe, but it's a real option.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the kids in all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Zoe is ten and Leo is seven, so the school side is not urgent, but I'd tell them honestly that things are changing. I'd tell my children that I'm not afraid, I'm busy, and that's a different thing. I'd want them to see us doing something about it.

say: I'd say we need **emergency rules**: income support and retraining on full pay.
Adaptability is useless if there are **no jobs** to adapt into.
think: I think **most of my job**; buying is reading, judging and negotiating.
do: Cut spending and build **six months** in cash.
Start a small **import label** built on my farmer relationships.
Ask Dan to retrain for something **hands-on**, like building surveying.
feel: **Anxious**, but busy, and she'd rather act than stare at it.
S2.quote: I'd tell my children that I'm not afraid, I'm busy, and that's a different thing.
fieldNote: She gambles on **personal trust** with farmers, the one thing a machine can't copy.
Her adaptability gives **action**, not calm; the mood is anxious by her own account.
The **hands-on retraining** idea for Dan shows she's reading the 3-year gap.

steps.text: Cut unneeded spending and build six months of cash
Import small single-origin lots under my own label
Ask Dan to retrain in hands-on building surveying
Pay for a second year of tasting qualifications

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's long enough to build something, short enough to feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real window. At work I'd push to use it, retrain people, rebuild roles, and not pretend it's not coming. With friends I'd be honest that it worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I could ride the first three years on my skills, then it gets thin. I'd want to be on the right side of it before it hits, which means owning something or being someone clients ask for by name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first year to learn the heavy stuff: build the forecasting system properly, maybe study some data analysis. I'd begin the import label as a side thing on weekends. And I'd get our savings to six months, with the mortgage balance down by a decent chunk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but ambitious. It's like a deadline: stressful but it focuses me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want to be someone clients ask for by name. How do you build that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By being visible: tasting events, a newsletter, showing up at the farms. Customers should think of me, not of the company. It sounds a bit self-promoting, but in a world where a machine can negotiate, a person with a name and a track record is the thing that's left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Evenings and weekends, for a couple of years. Dan would have to carry more at home, and we'd have to agree it's worth it. I'd trade a few years of Saturdays for a job that can't be done by a machine.

say: I'd say **five years** is a real window and we should use it.
With friends I'd admit it **worries** me.
think: I could ride the first **three years** on my skills, then it gets thin.
I want to be someone clients **ask for by name**, or own something.
do: Build the forecasting system **properly** and study some data analysis.
Get savings to six months and cut the **mortgage balance**.
feel: **Uneasy** but ambitious; the deadline focuses me.
S3.quote: I'd trade a few years of Saturdays for a job that can't be done by a machine.
fieldNote: She turns the warning time into **personal branding** for a human-trust job.
The cost is **family time**, and she's open about asking Dan to carry it.
Her mood stays **uneasy** because she expects to keep her job for years.

steps.text: Study data analysis in the evenings for a year
Start importing small lots as a weekend side business
Cut the mortgage balance and reach six months saved

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long runway. I'd call that almost comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough to adapt as long as people actually start. I'd tell friends who are less comfortable with tech to get going now, not in nine years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm fairly relaxed. By then the kids are 17 and 20, the mortgage will be mostly paid, and I'll have had ten years to build a name. I'd actually find it exciting to have a front-row seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools daily, run the import side project to see if it grows, and keep saving. I'd also invest some money in index funds, since a decade gives me time. I'd help Dan plan a move into something that suits him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of curiosity. It feels like a story I'm in, not one that happens to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the mortgage will be mostly paid. How does that change your thinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A paid-off house is a safety net. If I could cover housing, I could try bolder things: start a business, take a lower-paid job I like. It turns the whole thing from a danger into a choice. That's what ten years buys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this version that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who won't use the decade. I worry less about myself and more about the buyers who never touch the tools because it feels too far off to matter. I'd try to pull a few of them along.

say: I'd say a **decade** is enough to adapt if people actually start.
I'd tell less comfortable friends to get going **now**.
think: I'm fairly relaxed; the kids will be older and the **mortgage mostly paid**.
I'd find it **exciting** to have a front-row seat.
do: Keep using the tools daily and grow the **import side project**.
Put money into **index funds**, since a decade gives time.
Help Dan plan a **move** into work that suits him.
feel: **Calm**, curious; it feels like a story she's in, not one done to her.
S4.quote: I worry less about myself and more about the buyers who never touch the tools because it feels too far off to matter.
fieldNote: A **paid-off house** turns danger into choice, in her telling.
Her worry is for **others** who won't use the time, not for herself.
She's the clearest example in this set of **comfort with change**.

steps.text: Put 150 a month into index funds
Grow the import label into a proper small business
Help Dan plan a move into project management

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It's too quick for even an adaptable person to rebuild. Dan and I are both in jobs a machine could do, and we'd have to change both at once. What would help is income support while we retrain, and companies being honest about timelines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that being comfortable with technology doesn't make me safe. I use these tools every day, and that's exactly why I know how much of my own job they could do. It makes me a clear-eyed optimist, not a confident one.

headlineQuote: I use these tools every day, and that's exactly why I know how much of my own job they could do.
portrait: Chloe Petrov, 43, is **senior buyer** at a coffee and tea importer, with an architect husband, two school-age children and a mortgage.
Progressive and adaptive: uses AI **every day** and turns change into action quickly.
Only about **two months** saved, and both her job and Dan's are desk-based, which sits under the optimism.
Calm in the plateau and the ten-year world, **anxious** in the 2028 case.
Her plan is to lean on **farmer trust**: a side import label and being a buyer clients name.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario, because she and Dan would have to change careers at once.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support** while retraining and honest timelines from companies.
